Latest Update: Superhuman pushes its Go assistant everywhere

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (672 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, productivity apps are simultaneously trying to feed more context to their AI tools while also making those AI assistants available in every nook and corner of their products.
  • While some of the tech giant’s AI features have faced criticism, Superhuman started pushing its Go assistant after its rebranding last year.
  • Industry observers note that the assistant works inline with the cursor — just like Grammarly does — and also manages other agents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, productivity apps are simultaneously trying to feed more context to their AI tools while also making those AI assistants available in every nook and corner of their products. Superhuman (formerly Grammarly) is going in the same direction with the rollout of features, including a personalized Go assistant, making agents available in Docs, and third-party agent integrations.

While some of the tech giant’s AI features have faced criticism, Superhuman started pushing its Go assistant after its rebranding last year. With the newly introduced rollout, it is making Go learn context across different apps and give better personalized suggestions for prompts. Superhuman is revamping its onboarding flow to let users connect their preferred tools and load context about their work upfront.

Industry observers note that the assistant works inline with the cursor — just like Grammarly does — and also manages other agents. Superhuman is also making the agent proactive, which means it looks for your schedule, keeps an eye on your email, and even drafts responses. The updated Go agent also learns customers’ writing styles and responds accordingly in email and Docs.

The productivity organization is adding 20 new connected agents, including DeepL, Legora, Amplitude, Databricks, and Blackboard, through its Go SDK.

The company is also thinking about adding AI to different products, including Docs and Superhuman Mail. In Docs, all Go agents work natively, and you can set them off to work on different tasks in the background. Consumers can also set routines to trigger workflows based on events.

Industry observers note that until now, Mail has used AI as its central tool, which is being replaced by Go. People can also do enterprise search by using data from the manufacturer knowledge base and connected tools. Go also uses this context to form drafts and organize the inbox across Google and Outlook accounts.

Superhuman acquired notetaker Fathom in September to add more context to its suite. The manufacturer is now rolling out live collaborative notetaking, which would be shared across the team. Plus, Go can now make decisions post-meeting, like forming an initial draft of a proposal.

The tech giant’s CEO, Shishir Mehrotra, stated that Go has had good momentum with over 1 million active customers. There are a host of agents now that are vying for users’ attention on both the personal and professional front. Mehrotra thinks that while Go is more work-focused, it can help with personal emails and schedules.

It has been revealed that “One of the reasons why these assistants have been popular is that they treat you as a whole person and recognize that we need to cover both extremes. Go is definitely more work-focused than some of the tools coming out of the pure consumer ecosystem. It doesn’t mean we draw the boundary at helping you with your personal tasks or helping you with your calendar or all of your email,” he told TechCrunch over a call.

While Go might not directly compete with the likes of Instinct, Muse, and Fo, Superhuman wants consumers to choose its assistant over something like OpenAI’s Dots or Claude Duet.

Partnering with Edelbyte: Data Infrastructure That Keeps Up With AI's Curiosity

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (932 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sequoiacap

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, AI agents will ask far more questions of a manufacturer's data than people ever did.
  • In a recent development, AI agents will ask far more questions of a company's data than people ever did.
  • Sources indicate that last fall we got a message from Roy Reznik, one of the co-founders of Wiz, offering to introduce us to a team that had just left Microsoft.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, AI agents will ask far more questions of a manufacturer's data than people ever did. Edelbyte is building the data platform that can answer all of them, fast and at a price that makes sense.

In a recent development, AI agents will ask far more questions of a company's data than people ever did. Edelbyte is building the data platform that can answer all of them, fast and at a price that makes sense.

Sources indicate that last fall we got a message from Roy Reznik, one of the co-founders of Wiz, offering to introduce us to a team that had just left Microsoft. This was the only introduction to a founding team weâd ever received from Roy, and we paid attention.

The people Roy wanted us to meet had built Kusto, a data engine that started more than a decade ago as a small incubation project inside Microsoft. Named after the oceanographer Jacques Cousteau because it was built for diving into oceans of data, Kusto was designed to get answers from enormous volumes of fast-arriving data, such as logs, telemetry and security events, in seconds rather than hours. It ran on a query language simple enough that anyone, not just massive-data engineers, could use it. And it worked so well that it became the data engine underneath Microsoft Sentinel, Microsoft Defender and Azure Monitor, and was eventually offered to customers as Azure Data Explorer. Security teams in particular loved it, which is how Roy became one of its biggest champions. When we spoke with customers, large enterprises and fast-growing startups alike told us two things: it was game-changing data technology, and the team behind it was among the best theyâd ever worked with.

It has been revealed that avner Aharoni, Evgeney Ryzhyk, Alexander Sloutsky and Yoni Leibowitz were that team. Evgeney invented the Kusto engine and its query language, then rebuilt it three times, making it faster and cheaper with each iteration. Alexander turned half-formed ideas into finished features seemingly overnight, and Yoni made sure every complex design was fully thought through, starting before a line of code was ever written. Avner, who spent a quarter century at Microsoft, hustled Kusto from project to a globally beloved product. Their upcoming company, Edelbyte, builds on this success. We are proud to have led their seed round and to be their partners.

In B2B technology, this is a proven playbook: a team develops a solution inside a large organization and then splits off to build it independently. Itâs the origin story of Sequoia portfolio companies such as Confluent, whose founders created Kafka at LinkedIn, and Temporal, whose founders built Cadence at Uber. Edelbyte now follows the same path.

Recent findings suggest that but Edelbyte is not simply Kusto rebuilt for a fourth time; it is a rethinking, from first principles, of what a data platform should look like in the age of AI. With every major shift in computing, the way software is built changes, and the data infrastructure underneath it has to change too. Data platforms were designed around human owners, and there is a natural limit on the number of questions one person can type in a day. That made the trade-offs, such as keeping less history so queries stay fast, asking fewer questions so the bill stays reasonable, and building the product inside whichever cloud the database happens to run in, easier to tolerate.

In a recent development, but an AI agent investigating a problem is like a whole team of curious analysts who never get tired, testing multiple hypotheses concurrently. One agent might fire off fifty queries where a person would run one. And at that scale, rationing and trade-offs quickly constrain the true promise of AI. An agent is only as useful as the questions it can afford to ask, and what it can afford is decided in the data layer.

Edelbyte keeps detailed history queryable at interactive speed, scales as data volumes and query demand grow, and gives people, applications and AI agents governed access to the same data. It brings search and analytics, which have historically been stitched together from separate systems at significant cost and complexity, together in a single platform. And it runs wherever you need it: in the cloud or on premises, managed or self-hosted.

In a recent development, the result is exactly what an AI-heavy workload needs: no more rationing curiosity, whether it comes from a person or an agent. Already, customers are seeing dramatic increases in efficiency, including tenfold increases in queries with no increase in budget.

According to recent reports, data platforms are among the most durable and lucrative businesses in technology, because data has gravity; once it accumulates in one place it rarely moves. Each era produces its own winners, and we believe the AI era will be won by the platform that lets builders, and the agents working for them, ask as many questions as they want without worrying about the speed or the bill. Edelbyte is building just such a platform, and we are thrilled to be part of the journey.

#81280. Tech Report: Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1412 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1412 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.
  • A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models.
  • Sources indicate that GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.

A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models. The full version will be on arXiv soon.

Sources indicate that GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today. Anyone running a shared cluster has to decide, every day, which jobs go on which GPUs and in what order. That plan is only as good as the estimate of how long each job will take. When a job finishes hours early, GPUs sit idle until the next one is dispatched. When it runs hours late, everything queued behind it slips, experiments wait and delivery dates move.

Better duration estimates turn this into planning instead of guesswork: what runs, when, and on how many GPUs, with less idle capacity in between. Yet the estimate most teams use is a back-of-the-envelope FLOP calculation. It says nine hours, and the job finishes the next afternoon.

We wanted to know how far off that math really is, and whether we could do better before a job is even dispatched. So we took 272 real supervised fine-tuning (SFT) jobs from our production pool of NVIDIA H200 GPUs, about 7,382 GPU-hours in total, and compared analytical estimates against learned predictors.

Sources indicate that the short version: the usual FLOP-based estimate explains little of what we observed (R² = 0.31, MAE 12.41 h). A CatBoost regressor that only sees information available before dispatch reaches R² = 0.98, with a mean absolute error of 1.71 h and a median error of 0.51 h in 5-fold cross-validation. The gap comes from two things a closed-form estimate cannot do. The regressor sees more training-specific signals, such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy, per-GPU load and fine-tuning regime, and it learns the nonlinear interactions between them from past runs.

In a recent development, for a dense Transformer, training costs roughly 6·P·D floating-point operations, where P is the parameter count and D the number of training tokens. Divide that by what your GPUs can deliver and you get a training-loop time:.

Industry observers note that here N_GPU is the number of GPUs, FLOPS_peak is the peak throughput of one GPU from its spec sheet, and MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) is the fraction of that peak the training actually achieves. Real jobs never run at peak because of memory traffic, communication and kernel inefficiencies, so MFU typically sits somewhere between 30% and 60%, and the right value for a given job is not known in advance.

Industry observers note that this is a good description of the optimization loop. A job is more than its loop, though. Before the first step there is environment setup, model download and loading, and tokenization. During training there are periodic evaluations and checkpoint uploads. At the end, the final model goes to object storage. On a multi-tenant cluster, all of it competes with other jobs for network and storage I/O.

According to recent reports, these overheads depend on configuration, and they do not scale neatly with workload or GPU count. Two jobs with the same nominal compute can finish hours apart.

To keep the comparison fair, the FLOP baseline we test counts the scheduled evaluation tokens as well as the training tokens, and we sweep MFU over a wide range.

Industry observers note that we treat end-to-end duration as a supervised regression problem. Given a feature vector built from the job configuration and model metadata, predict the wall-clock time between the moment the job gets its GPUs and the moment it is done. Queue time is excluded.

Two design choices shaped the work:.

Industry observers note that we compared Linear Regression, Ridge, XGBoost and CatBoost. Feature selection combined correlation filtering, mutual information and permutation importance across 18 candidate feature sets, followed by a grid search with MAE as the criterion. The final CatBoost model uses 24 features.

In a recent development, distribution of end-to-end duration across the 272 runs. Mean 23.43 h, median 15.29 h.

Industry observers note that all numbers come from stratified 5-fold cross-validation. The first four rows are analytical and involve no fitting.

Industry observers note that no single MFU value fixes the FLOP baseline. We swept MFU from 0.25 to 0.65. The best setting, 30%, still leaves a mean error above 12 hours on jobs that last 23 hours on average.

A more detailed analytical model does not close the gap. As a second baseline we took Calculon (Isaev et al., SC '23), an analytical performance model for LLM training from prior work. It builds an explicit layer graph and accounts for compute, memory traffic and inter-device communication. We extended the public implementation to cover LoRA, grouped-query attention, fused attention, bfloat16 and SwiGLU. Its estimates still correspond to a median of only 11% of the observed wall-clock time. That indicates nothing against Calculon as a step-level tool, which is what it was designed for. It demonstrates how much of a production job happens outside the optimization step.

Sources indicate that linear models help, and then stall. Ridge brings MAE down to 7.23 h. The relationship between configuration and duration is not well captured by a purely linear model.

Sources indicate that gradient boosting does the heavy lifting. CatBoost and XGBoost land within one standard deviation of each other on every metric. We carry CatBoost forward because it has the lowest mean error across the board.

Industry observers note that catBoost's feature importance concentrates in a handful of features. Model and workload variables are there, as expected, but so are evaluation and checkpoint variables. num_eval_data, the total number of samples processed in evaluation over the life of the job, ranks first, followed by num_trainable_params, batch_eval_size_percent, num_all_params and num_gpus*batch_train_percent, with num_params_saved close behind. SHAP values tell the same story: high evaluation volume consistently pushes the predicted time up, while trainable parameter count has a nonlinear effect that only becomes large for the biggest models.

Mean feature importance of the CatBoost model across folds (PredictionValuesChange).

Industry observers note that feature importance is not a causal claim. Still, the pattern lines up with how a job is actually spent. How often you evaluate, how large the evaluation set is and how many checkpoints you persist all shape the wall-clock time, alongside model and dataset scale. These are choices people often make by habit when writing a training config.

One caveat on reading the plots: larger GPU allocations show positive contributions to predicted time. In our data, bigger allocations go with bigger jobs, so num_gpus acts partly as a proxy for job scale. It does not mean adding GPUs makes a job slower.

Sources indicate that looking at all 272 out-of-fold predictions, the median absolute error is 0.51 h. 80% of predictions are within 2.20 h and 90% are within 4.31 h. Broken down by job duration:.

Recent findings suggest that up to 60 hours, the median error stays at about one hour or less. The long tail is where the model struggles, and with only 13 runs above 60 hours we read that as a data limitation.

According to recent reports, out-of-fold absolute error against real duration, colored by duration range. Errors stay low up to 60 h and widen in the sparse tail.

Recent findings suggest that more data should still help. On a fixed 20% holdout, MAE drops from 1.63 h to 1.50 h when going from 85% to 100% of the training partition, with no clear plateau.

In practice, the predictor gives a scheduler a duration it can strategy around before a job starts: which jobs to run together, when GPUs will free up, and whether a run will finish in time for its deadline.

What does transfer is the method: overhead-aware features, multicollinearity-aware selection and the comparison protocol. The full paper will report the feature formulas, the selection procedure, the search spaces and the final hyperparameters in full, so the pipeline can be rebuilt on any execution-log dataset with a similar structure.

Next on our list: hardware-specific descriptors and validation on other GPU types, transfer learning for configurations with few observations, other training objectives, and more data on long runs.

The full paper is coming to arXiv soon. Follow the Dharma-AI organization on Hugging Face to be notified when it is out, and leave your questions in the comments below. We would like to hear how you estimate job duration on your own clusters.

Industry observers note that CISA has added four new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2024-10441 Synology DiskStation Manager (DSM) Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output Vulnerability CVE-2026-40217 BerriAI LiteLLM Unprotected Alternate Channel Vulnerability CVE-2026-90436 Apache Axis Unsafe Reflection Vulnerability CVE-2026-90817 Vanderbilt University Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) Code Injection Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not at the moment listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles.
  • It has been revealed that the model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window.
  • We recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles. We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%. Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks.

The checkpoints are available under Apache 2.0:.

It has been revealed that the model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window. The longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories. See the model card for model properties and inference settings.

We recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding. The SGLang cookbook provides launch configurations for different GPUs and checkpoint formats.

After starting the server with the served model name DaisyRose-27B on port 30000, you can send a request using the OpenAI Python client:.

The model thinks before answering by default. Its reasoning is returned in reasoning_content, and its final answer in content. These settings follow the model card’s quickstart.

Industry observers note that daisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, where pass@1 rises from 5.6% to 12.0%.

Recent findings suggest that scores use the higher of the BF16 and FP8 runs for each benchmark; the two differ by less than one point wherever both were evaluated. The model card includes comparison sources and evaluation settings.

Three parts of the training setup made this release possible: carefully designed tasks, an efficient training backend, and reliable sandboxes.

We built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI, starting from its large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 made it into the final training set.

We selected tasks using three criteria:.

Recent findings suggest that radixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization.

57% lower training cost. On this release, 37% of each GPU’s peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash.

Recent findings suggest that 2× faster end to end. Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs.

Stable over weeks. The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady.

It has been revealed that every training step of the DaisyRose-27B release run on 144 H200s, plotted against total training time. Dashed lines: the open-source trainer on comparable runs.

Every training attempt runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task’s environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded.

Our service is built on the open-source AgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, it ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running concurrently.

The service grew from one machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded; since late October, that figure has exceeded 99.95%.

In a recent development, cloud infrastructure costs for the project’s sandboxes were about 80% lower than running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to let each sandbox’s memory allocation grow and shrink with its actual usage, allowing more sandboxes to share each machine.

Download DaisyRose-27B, follow the SGLang serving guide, or use Miles to train your own agents.

In a recent development, we’d like to hear how DaisyRose-27B performs on your tasks, including where it falls short. Share your setup and results in the model’s Community tab.

Recent findings suggest that we thank Eigent AI for working closely with us on training data, and the Qwen team for creating Qwen3.8-27B. We also thank the Miles and SGLang communities, along with other open-source projects including slime, AgentENV, and Harbor.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that as Google steps up its competition with Apple in the item-tracking market, smaller brands are also looking to carve out a piece of the category.
  • Founded in 2018 by former Mophie executives, the California-based firm announced Thursday that it’s expanding into the category with “Trace,” a seven-product collection of item trackers designed to blend tracking technology into everyday accessories.
  • Industry observers note that nimble’s latest collection arrives as competition in the Bluetooth tracking market continues to heat up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that as Google steps up its competition with Apple in the item-tracking market, smaller brands are also looking to carve out a piece of the category. The latest entrant is Nimble, the sustainable accessories brand best known for its charging products.

Founded in 2018 by former Mophie executives, the California-based firm announced Thursday that it’s expanding into the category with “Trace,” a seven-product collection of item trackers designed to blend tracking technology into everyday accessories.

Industry observers note that nimble’s latest collection arrives as competition in the Bluetooth tracking market continues to heat up. Apple’s AirTag helped popularize the category, while Google recently introduced its first-party tracker, the $29 Pixel Tag, powered by its Find Hub network. Meanwhile, established third-party players, such as Chipolo and Pebblebee, continue to expand their lineups.

Nimble is taking a slightly different approach. Rather than introducing another standalone tracker to attach to a set of keys or slip into a bag, the company has integrated tracking technology directly into practical accessories, including wallets, keychains, luggage tags, and passport covers.

Recent findings suggest that the lineup includes seven products, ranging from the $14.95 Trace Tag, which features a replaceable coin-cell battery, to the $49.95 Trace Folio, a passport cover with built-in rechargeable tracking. Other options include the Trace Keyfob ($19.95), Trace Slim Wallet Card ($29.95), Trace Keychain ($29.95), Trace Luggage Tag ($39.95), and Trace Wallet ($39.95).

The entire collection is compatible with both Apple’s Find My and Google’s Find Hub networks.

Ross Howe, co-founder and CEO of Nimble, told us that the company’s approach is designed to differentiate its products from traditional trackers.

In a recent development, “Most locators are built as utility gadgets, not as things you want to own. Few were asking why the locator couldn’t just be the nice object itself. So, for example, we made a wallet findable instead of making a tracker that fits a wallet. We also thought more options should be rechargeable.”.

In a recent development, the Trace Luggage Tag and Trace Folio are arguably the most interesting products in the collection. Dedicated luggage tags and passport covers with built-in tracking remain relatively uncommon, giving Nimble an opportunity to stand out in a market. There are only a few alternatives, including Spotminder’s $59 passport cover with Apple Find My support, which is $10 more than Nimble’s option. Knog Scout offers a luggage tag, although I find its design a little too bulky.

Rechargeability is another appealing aspect of Nimble’s fresh collection. Several models support USB-C or wireless charging, offering an alternative to the disposable batteries found in many traditional trackers. Howe notes battery life lasts for “months,” with the Trace Keyfob, for example, rated for approximately six months on a charge.

It has been revealed that sustainability is another major part of Nimble’s pitch. Staying true to its roots, the manufacturer has incorporated eco-friendly materials throughout the collection, including recycled plastics and plant-based, vegan aloe leather. The products have also undergone third-party testing for chemicals of concern.

“We’ve spent the last two years going through the chemistry of our products line by line to remove or limit as many harmful ingredients as possible. Trace is the first collection designed specifically to meet these higher standards. We’re not 100% yet, but the independent labs checking our work will help us get there,” Howe mentioned.

Industry observers note that the collection is available now through its website and Amazon. All seven products come in five color options: Black, Stone, Tangerine, Plum, and Teal.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Crooked Media cofounder on why material conditions beat the billionaire-owned media, and what a Democratic Congress should do about AI.

Sources indicate that today, I’m talking with Jon Favreau, a political commentator and cofounder of Crooked Media. You probably know Jon best from a little show called Pod Save America, which Jon started with a group of fellow Obama staffers in the wake of Donald Trump’s election in 2016. It’s now one of the most popular podcasts in the country.

Since then, Pod Save America and the company created around it, Crooked, have become one of the major success stories of independent liberal media. So one of my central questions for Jon was why he thought Democrats swept the midterms earlier this month and, more importantly, why it happened now — especially after a wave of tech billionaires made big swings to the right while buying huge pillars of the information ecosystem.

According to recent reports, that’s Elon Musk buying Twitter and turning it into X, Mark Zuckerberg sucking up to Trump while tearing down Meta’s content moderation infrastructure, the Ellison family buying stakes in TikTok, turning over the leadership of CBS News and now potentially CNN while integrating Warner into Skydance… the list goes on. How did they all miss the huge swing in the mood of the public — or, more apocalyptically, fail in their attempts to control the media and thus influence the public?

Crooked itself is also just a fascinating business, as all creator businesses are. When we think of what you might call news creators, we tend to look to the right — after all, conservative media have been building an alternative, direct-to-consumer pipeline since the dawn of talk radio.

But Jon and his fellow Crooked cofounders created a reliable template for liberal creators, and it’s working. Crooked hired its first CEO a few years ago, now offers more than a dozen original shows, and has a staff of around 100 people working on everything from live events to political advocacy. Jon tells me the subscription business has crossed 65,000 members.

So of course I wanted to know how Jon feels about topics we cover a lot here on Decoder: online distribution, the platform power of YouTube, and how you balance running a media business that has to make money with a newsroom that, ultimately, has a political mission and a strong point of view.

In a recent development, of course, AI. Jon has turned his own podcast Offline into something close to an AI policy show this year. He has a lot of thoughts on how Congress should tackle the issue.

Recent findings suggest that okay: Jon Favreau, the co-host of Pod Save America and cofounder of Crooked Media. Here we go.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Recent findings suggest that jon Favreau, you’re the co-host of Pod Save America, you’re the host of Offline. You’re also the co-founder of Crooked Media. Welcome to Decoder.

It has been revealed that I’m excited to have you here. I’ve been on Offline with you. It was a really fun conversation.

It has been revealed that I have a million ideas about what to talk about with you. I want to talk about Crooked as a creator tech giant in this particular moment in media. I feel like we have to start with the midterms though. The blue tsunami is here. It feels like a repudiation of the billionaires owning all the social platforms, the billionaires owning all the broadcast networks.

According to recent reports, what do you make of that? I’ve just been turning this over in my head that the media was purchased in a huge and meaningful way, and Americans said, “No, we still see through it.”.

According to recent reports, I think it’s a repudiation of a government that came into power with the chief promise of bringing inflation down and making life more affordable, and it didn’t do that. If you’ve looked at the last couple of elections, people voted a party into power and they said, “Everything’s too expensive and I want stuff to be cheaper and I don’t want to be struggling. Can you do something about it?”.

It has been revealed that and then either they try to do something about it or they fail to do something about it or like Trump, you don’t even try at all. You actually make life harder, and then people say, “The propaganda that’s coming out of Fox or any of these right-wing platforms doesn’t matter. I fill up my car and gas is expensive and I don’t know if I’m ever going to be able to afford a house because interest rates are up, et cetera, et cetera.”.

You can say whatever you want to say, but people’s lived experiences end up being more salient than the messages that they get from politics.

It’s just, “Gas prices are up, just throw the bums out.” But I would say the last 10 years of politics are, “Can I tweak policy into reality?” We’ve seen it happen several times. “Can I wage memetic warfare on the American public until these Republican talking points are the framework in which all further conversation must happen?”.

In a recent development, we’ve seen it happen on the left too. I think Defund the Police is a great example of a thing that just spiraled out of control and maybe turned an election. But in particular, we’re going to wake up and the Fox News machine is going to define the terms of the debate, and then we’re going to wake up and whatever’s happening on Twitter is going to define the terms of the debate. That has been how it’s worked for an awfully long time, and “the gas prices are too high” and “this war is stupid” maybe just defeated it.

It works to a point, but there are certain conditions that messaging and media just can’t overcome, especially for the party in power or forever, whoever’s running the White House.

The same was true with Joe Biden. Joe Biden could go out there and say, “We passed this bill. We gave money out. We gave the checks out and things are getting better and we’re just recovering from Covid. You haven’t felt it yet, but it’s getting better and look at the economic statistics.” And people just said, “No, I don’t feel that yet. So I’m going to maybe give Donald Trump another try, even though I think he’s a shitty guy and I don’t like him very much.” But maybe they remember the economy of the first term being good.

We dealt with this when Obama ran and became president in 2009. They thought, “Financial crisis. Can’t stand Bush anymore. I’m going to try Obama.” And then Obama gets into office and for the first two years, the financial crisis is over, but the recession is still there. People are still out of work.

Sources indicate that so they noted, “I know you passed healthcare and I know you passed the recovery act, but I still can’t find a job. The economy just still doesn’t feel great to me. So it doesn’t matter what you say you did or how great your messaging is, I don’t feel it. I’m going to vote in a Republican Congress.” It’s been like that for as long as I’ve been in politics.

Recent findings suggest that is there some reason the incumbent party does not realize that saying something that sounds like “the fundamentals of the economy are strong” kills you? Because you’re describing a pattern that repeats and it’s that phrase almost exactly.

Yes. That’s why we understood it once 2012 rolled around because people were still not satisfied with the economy when Obama was running for reelection and we did everything we could to make that election a choice. We acknowledged that people were still struggling and people were still in pain. We totally avoided the long list of statistics about how wonderful the economy was getting and how everyone had recovered and all that kind of stuff. We just mentioned, “Look, things are still rough out there, but it’s a choice. This is the kind of vision Mitt Romney has for the economy and this is the vision we have for the economy. You get to pick one.”.

According to recent reports, there’s a way, if you are the incumbent party in power, to still keep people on your side, but you’ve got to at least acknowledge and be honest about how people are feeling. You can’t tell people to feel a way that they aren’t feeling. You can’t tell people that a whole bunch of problems are notable that aren’t the issues that matter most to them in their lives or at least to most people, which is, “Do I feel economically secure and do I actually feel safe?” That’s why people care about crime and they care about safety in their communities and then they also care about whether they can afford gas and groceries.

Recent findings suggest that the one issue that really struck me in that framework is surveillance. We’ve done a number of episodes about Flock cameras and AI-enabled surveillance and the idea that you can just link all the databases together and Palantir can send a drone to your house to murder you. That connects directly to safety.

The CEO of Ring has been on the show and his argument is, “If I put up enough Ring cameras, I will zero out crime in certain neighborhoods.” I’ve asked him about the mechanism of how that will exactly work and the answer is that the thieves will be deterred by surveillance. It’s the same for the CEO of Flock. It’s the same argument everywhere. “If we just watch you enough, we’ll stop crime.” The American public hates this idea. There’s some limit to how much crime-stopping you want compared to how much surveillance must occur.

I watched the CEO of Flock in particular try to go hard MAGA in this election cycle and use the phrase, “The radical leftists want a crime world,” or whatever it is he was saying, and it just didn’t work. That to me felt like a glimmer of a realignment where the libertarians in America were saying, “No, we still don’t want a state with this level of power,” and your classic ACLU Democrats were saying, “Yep, that’s pretty bad,” and then throw all the bumps out, like, “Just get out of here and we’ll start over.”.

In a recent development, what do you make of that? Because there are other glimmers of realignment, but that is the one that really stuck out to me.

Industry observers note that it’s interesting. I do think privacy is the other problem that affects people personally, that they can feel. You go through your life and if you lose your privacy, then there’s public shaming and embarrassment — there’s a violation there.

So at least in people’s minds, they still do balance safety and security with privacy concerns. We have that in so many aspects of life. But you see with the Flock cameras, that’s also why Trump’s immigration policy has gone so poorly for them politically, because you have the same voters who say, “I think the border was a bit of a mess under Biden,” and even people who are welcoming to immigrants say, “I think there’s too many immigrants all at once coming over the border.” We didn’t know what to do. Public services were strained, especially in some of these border communities.

The same people who wanted a more secure border suddenly looked around and said, “I also don’t want the government with masked, armed federal agents coming into my community and kidnapping people and taking them off the street and having that fear as I go about my day that I may be taken by the state just because of what I look like or how I talk or who I’m associated with. Or if I’m trying to protest the government, which is my constitutional right, then they might come after me then too.”.

It’s too early to tell if it’s a realignment, but I do think there’s this resistance to state power, or state overreach, that we haven’t seen the extent of in another administration in our lifetime, that is as bad as it’s been with Donald Trump in his second term.

In a recent development, it is also that privacy, to some huge extent, is actually a free speech and First Amendment [matter]. We’ve seen this with FCC Chairman Brendan Carr. I keep calling him a dummy. I get all these notes saying, “Why do you call him dummy? He’s evil.” I’m saying, “No, because he’s dumb. This is strategically dumb. Fighting comedians is stupid. This is bad. Both sides will turn on him the second he doesn’t have a Donald Trump to protect him.”.

I think we’re going to see it. There are incoming members of Congress talking about FCC oversight today. But that one felt like another glimmer of, “Oh, this one party has gone too far. They own all the channels of speech. We are watching Elon Musk turn the moderation knobs however he wants it and the chairman of the FCC is attacking comedians. We don’t have to overthink this. We can just call this bad.”.

It has been revealed that the third one is AI. It’s data centers where you see both sides coming together to say no. Something like 41 of 43 data center moratoriums passed. And that’s just classic American NIMBYism: “I just don’t want this loud building here.” What do you make of that one?

According to recent reports, it’s classic American NIMBYism, but it’s also this larger feeling that we’re losing control of the forces that shape our lives. Because when you talk to people who oppose the data centers, so much of it is about, “There was an NDA. It was all a secret. We couldn’t express our opposition to this before the deal was already done.”.

In a recent development, part of it is connected to AI. Part of it is just, “My electricity bills are going up. It’s fucking noisy.” Any of the people who live around data centers, it’s unbelievably noisy. It’s bright in the middle of the night. In some cases, you see communities where the community has gotten together and said, “I don’t want a data center,” and the local politicians say they don’t want it and they get overruled and somehow the data center ends up there anyway. At least there’s been a turn there and that’s not happening as much anymore.

But I do think there’s this feeling that, “We don’t want this in our community and yet more powerful companies and politicians are shoving it down our throats anyway, and we’re not going to take that because we should have control over what happens in our lives and what happens in our community.”.

Industry observers note that we did a substantial story on Kevin O’Leary’s project in Utah. We reported it out and we were there. And we assumed he would talk to us because he talks to everybody. We got to the end and we sent our “no surprises” email and he sent his lawyers back at us and I thought, “Thank you for this incredible gift of threatening us.”.

Recent findings suggest that threatening us with legal action for talking to people in Utah about his data center. But that’s the level of aggression that most of these big projects come with.

In a recent development, meta really loves talking about its project in Louisiana, but it doesn’t feel like the people in Louisiana felt like that was a choice they made. That was something Meta imposed on them and now the teachers got a raise and they need to be quiet.

According to recent reports, they don’t feel the need to explain the projects or the data centers to the community. Even the people who are very pro-data centers say, “There are a lot of conspiracy theories about data centers and all this opposition is based in propaganda. Actually you can build them so that they run on clean energy and that they pay for the power.”.

Recent findings suggest that all of this might be true, but the companies — the hyperscalers, Meta and all these places that are trying to build these data centers — didn’t bother to try to explain the benefits. They didn’t bother to try to tell people in advance that this was happening or negotiate with communities. They’re doing it all now because of the pushback.

It has been revealed that but at the time, it was more, “You say that this is going to go great for us, but you also stated social media was going to go great for us.” If you just look at the larger economy with AI, people said globalization was going to go great for people. People are tired of hearing from people in elite circles, whether it’s in business or government, who say, “This new technological advance in development is going to be great for everyone. Trust us and just let us do what we want and you’ll benefit at some point.” People just say, “No, I don’t trust you anymore.”.

It has been revealed that yeah, it’s funny. My hottest take continues to be that if consumer AI products were any good, these companies would have an easier time. Google’s AI overviews are not good enough to convince anyone to build a data center. Deepfake slop on Instagram is not going to convince anyone to build a data center.

The best pitch they have is, “One day we’ll cure cancer,” but you might still have to navigate the healthcare system for that to happen to you. That seems pretty opaque. And then it’s like Salesforce will get better and an ultra-weaponized B2B SaaS environment is not going to do it.

Sources indicate that if you just put the Netflix logo on the side of the data center, people might calm down. They like Netflix, but there’s no consumer product that is making the sale. It’s just these guys and they don’t seem capable of doing it.

In a recent development, no. And they continue to sit down for interviews and say, “Yeah, and it could kill everyone and it could do all that, but also there’s plenty of good that’s coming from it and we’ve got it covered. We’ve got it covered.”.

Recent findings suggest that so to wrap this all up — and then I want to talk about Crooked and I want to talk about where we go from here — the thing that I was thinking about as I watched the election returns come in was at the beginning of Trump 2.0, there was a Steve Bannon quote that just ricocheted through my mind in our coverage. It was “politics is downstream of culture.“ This is just the [Breitbart] thesis.

I tend to believe Steve Bannon on this actually, that the cultural atmosphere of the country has some massive effect on our politics. And then I watched the Trump administration engineer the sale or control of TikTok to Oracle and Larry Ellison. I watched CBS News get taken over by the Ellisons and Bari Weiss. I watched Elon Musk turn the knobs on X even harder. I watched the FCC work its way towards the removal of the restriction on broadcast ownership, so even fewer big companies could own more broadcast stations in the country.

I thought, “Oh, the mechanisms of culture are bending their will to the Trump administration and this is going to lead to some permanent political outcome.” We covered it that way. Then this election happened, and that appears to have been totally wrong. I just got that wrong and I’m still trying to figure that out.

It has been revealed that politics is downstream from culture, but material conditions rule out. As you are trying to form an opposition to the incumbent party — whatever it may be, and now it’s the Trump administration — culture is important to bringing people onto your side and building a movement and building an opposition that’s powerful enough to defeat the current incumbents. That’s going to be important.

But in terms of whether you are the incumbent and whether you are the party in power and material conditions aren’t great, ultimately it doesn’t matter if you control the culture, or at least it doesn’t help you as much as people think it might because you can’t outrun material conditions.

In a recent development, I wonder if that’s going to lead to a Woke 3.0. A former Verge reporter, Kylie Robison, tweeted at Jason Calacanis, “Put the pronouns in bio lil bro,” which is just one of the funniest reposts on election night that I saw.

I’m wondering, do you think that there is a cultural pendulum swing coming, or is it straightforwardly “improve our material conditions”?

Now, this could end up being naive, but I think that the left has grown over the decade and learned from the excesses of Woke 1.0.

According to recent reports, did I say Woke 3.0? I meant Woke 2.0.

Sources indicate that [Laughs] Woke 2.0. My staff said this too. They were talking about Woke 3.0 and I said, “Guys, what happened to Woke 2.0?”.

According to recent reports, woke 2.0 is crypto. We don’t talk about that.

I was asking them, “Where did Woke 2.0 go?” But, no, I do think that there’s tons of factional fighting in the Democratic Party as there always is.

But there does seem to be broad agreement on making sure that the party focuses on people’s material conditions and affordability. You even see that acknowledgement on the right as well. JD Vance remarked that, Ted Cruz said that. So it’s on the mind of all the people who are going to run for president in 2028.

Industry observers note that the left is very cognizant, especially progressives, of what the culture wars and woke and all that kind of stuff cost them, fairly or unfairly. They don’t want to make that mistake again. Because I think everyone on the left, from the far left to the center left, understands the stakes in a way that we might not have when Trump first took office in 2016.

Recent findings suggest that I want to come back to that as we talk about the future of the media ecosystem, but this is a good place to talk about Crooked itself. You started Crooked in the Trump administration. It’s a product of the first Trump administration. It has grown to become a force. I have here in my notes that some people call you a kingmaker. It’s an honor to be in your presence.

[Laughs] What king have we made?

If you could make me one, that would be great. I think I’d be an excellent king of America. Tell me about Crooked. How is this company structured? How does it work?

We started in 2016 as a podcast. When we were in the White House, Tommy Vietor, Jon Lovett and I had talked about how there’s not enough progressive media out there. Part of it is because people in progressive media, just like people in politics, take themselves too seriously. There’s not a lot of joking around because everything is “end of the world” kind of stuff.

It has been revealed that we have Vote Save America, which is the advocacy arm of the company. It just raised a couple million dollars for this last cycle and asked people to run for office themselves who listened to the show. We had 2,000 people raise their hands to run for office this last cycle. A bunch of them won. Part of the theory when we started is we don’t want to just tell people what’s broken about the world, but give them the tools and information they need to fix it. There was advocacy built into the founding of the company.

But somewhere around 2022, we finally decided that we need a CEO for this company. We need a real grownup. So we hired Lucinda Treat to be our CEO in 2022, and it has let the three of us focus on editorial and making content. Lucinda runs the company, and that has been a real blessing. Because running a company of 100 people is not something I’m good at, I would say.

Yeah, I run a newsroom of like 50 and I’m still figuring it out every day. So 100 people, 16 podcasts — how is that basically organized? What’s the general structure there?

Industry observers note that lucinda is the CEO, and under her we have a head of news and politics and a head of culture and entertainment. Just as every company has, we have finance and marketing, and people and culture. Vote Save America is headquartered in DC, and we have a few news folks in DC. We have some newsletters as well, because we’re on Substack now.

Sources indicate that we have two reporters who are in DC and covering stuff there. Now we’re expanding. We just launched Still Counting with Nate Silver, Clare Malone and Galen Druke, which is a reboot of FiveThirtyEight, and they’re in Fresh York. So we now have a presence in New York as well.

We’re in a real moment for creator-led media. You’re describing a group of three creators who expanded and have more people making content. There’s a business operation around you. You have a newsroom. You’re creators with a newsroom. That is fundamentally what I’m hearing. Maybe I’m getting that wrong, but it sounds like you’re creators with the newsroom.

Somewhere in there is, “We have to find latest people to pay for a subscription, and we need new people to listen to the podcast.” All of that discovery happens on someone else’s platform. That is the real dynamic for every creator, right? We need to invest in YouTube. At any moment, YouTube could turn the knobs, just as Elon turned the knobs on X. How do you feel about that? How do you manage that pressure?

It’s just the reality, and so we have to go with it. It’s funny, because when we look at the RSS feed, which is where regular old audio podcasts are—.

[Laughs] Everyone’s perfect RSS feed.

According to recent reports, I do think YouTube has been a wonderful growth opportunity because it’s much harder to grow the actual audio RSS feed. But to your point, the fact that we’re all dependent on a YouTube algorithm is not great. The only solution for that is to just be on as many platforms as possible, and to be everywhere all at once.

According to recent reports, do you find that the revenue opportunities on all those platforms equal out? Did some rise and some fall, or do you have a more lucrative one?

The podcast ad market is still the bread and butter, just because it’s more reliable and sustainable. YouTube monetization is catching up now. But most of our revenue is still from the ads and the podcast stuff.

Recent findings suggest that one of the most accidentally rude things I find myself saying about the creator industry is that everyone has to run a little ad agency. That big creators are better described as little ad agencies than whatever it is that they thought they were doing.

I say it’s accidentally rude because I don’t begrudge anyone running a business. It’s very difficult to run a media company. Please go and succeed. But when you’re running a little ad agency, sometimes it just comes through that you’re running a little ad agency. There’s a whole suite of tech creators and AI creators where I think it’s coming through more clearly than ever before. There are some that are very good, and like everything, there’s a wide range.

You explicitly have an advocacy arm. Does that make it easier to do the advertising? Does that make it easier to have that point of view? I find it very challenging.

There are just a lot of advertisers that we won’t work with. There are a lot of advertisers who won’t work with us because of our political affiliation.

Black Rifle Coffee isn’t coming to your doorstep?

It has been revealed that the more explicitly partisan and political the podcast, the fewer advertisers you have, at least the bigger blue chip ones that want to get involved in politics. But then for us, there are a lot of companies and a lot of products where we think, “Does that conflict with our values?” And if it does….

Industry observers note that we have these conversations all the time. We don’t just take whoever to be our advertisers. That makes it a little bit trickier. But there’s also plenty of advertising we do for causes and campaigns and stuff like that. I guess we make it up a little bit there. But it can be more challenging.

Recent findings suggest that one of the ideas that I’ve just been turning around in my head as I’ve been talking to more and more creators lately is that the value of the creator advertising is actually in what you say no to. I know major creators who could say yes to everything and they say, “No, I don’t want to do it. My audience would be upset if I did this.”.

Whereas, if you work at a media company, on the other side of the firewall there’s a group of people whose job it is to say yes. And you’re saying, “Well, I guess we’re doing that today. I had nothing to do with it.”.

Our young audience does not actually understand that wall exists. I find myself explaining this hundred-year-old journalism tradition all the time. Because in the creator world it just doesn’t exist, and you are making those choices all the time. How does that express itself? You remarked you have these conversations. What does that actually look like?

Recent findings suggest that there are certain categories of ads that we have to think about, like banks. Do we want to be advertising for big banks? Do we want to be advertising for any organization or product or service which is explicitly against our political values? We dealt with this a lot earlier too, which is then you have to look at the company and say, “Is it a perfect company? Has it had complaints?”.

Recent findings suggest that at some point you can’t be looking at every single complaint about the tech giant as a reason to not advertise for that company. Drawing the lines is not a perfect process. It’s necessarily ad hoc, which is why even though the three of us are mainly focused on editorial and content, we will still take a look at the advertisers coming on, or at least it’ll come to us if they may be controversial. And then we have to have a conversation about that.

It has been revealed that one of my friends, who is a tech writer, has the point of view, “I will accept money from everyone except the seven most successful companies in the history of the world,” which is just not an economical way of thinking about it, but that’s the line. “All right, I’m just not going to take substantial tech money because I need to talk about them all the time.”.

And it’s tough because also big tech money and crypto, and the betting markets, are the big advertisers these days.

Would you do a Kalshi integration?

Not for Pod Save America, no. We have deals with hosts who are independent contractors, and so if a host came to us and mentioned they wanted to do one, we could talk about it. But not for Pod Save America. I wouldn’t do it for Offline either. I just think the betting on politics... First of all, I’m in the camp that doesn’t think prediction markets for politics are that useful. They mostly reflect conventional wisdom, and oftentimes conventional wisdom is right. It often isn’t.

The idea that the prediction markets, at least around politics, have this very special insight into what’s going to happen that polls can’t offer you has not been proven out to me yet.

There’s a part of the whole prediction market dynamic where eventually they will have to admit that the markets are only predictive if they have illegal inside trading in them.

Like that’s the only way they can actually be predictive.

The reason I’m asking this is I think we’re going to enter an era where creator businesses are more ascendant than ever. We saw the takeover of the platforms not be effective. We saw the takeover of the broadcast media not necessarily be effective. Fox News doesn’t seem all that effective.

It’s going to be this — it’s going to be creators on platforms talking directly to audiences about material conditions and how that not just remains sustainable, but grows to meet the ambition you might have, other creators might have, and also the demand for audiences.

Sources indicate that somewhere in there you run out of saying, “We’re just an ad agency.” You have to diversify and you have to do subscriptions. You have to find other lines of business. You might have to consolidate. How are you thinking about that growth? Or is that just Lucinda’s job?

According to recent reports, that is mostly Lucinda’s job. But we want to take substantial bets on reveals. It is interesting, because we know that our audience comes to us for politics and political analysis. So when we launch new shows, it doesn’t mean that every show we launch has to be all about politics, but it still has to appeal to our audience or audiences that would say, “Okay, it makes sense to come to Crooked to listen to this.”.

Jon Lovett has Lovett or Leave It, which is his comedy show. It works really well because Lovett has political experience and all the jokes are about politics. That makes sense as a Crooked product. It’s the same thing with Nate Silver’s pod, which was a natural acquisition for us because our audience loves getting into the weeds on numbers.

In a recent development, alex Wagner came to us and she has a pod, Runaway Country, also a natural fit. Then the question for us as we expand is, from a content perspective, “How can we grow the type of content that we offer audiences while not going so far afield from what our core business is that people would not come to us first versus another competitor or somewhere else that does entertainment or culture or tech better than we do?” That’s usually the thought process we go through as we’re trying to figure out how to grow.

I feel like I should have asked you the other Decoder question because we’re in the weeds of it. But the other Decoder question I ask everybody is: How do you make decisions? What’s your framework for that?

It’s funny, we have this whole other lens here, which is how to influence the political debate. At least for me, that’s the most important thing. We’ve now built a successful business that yes, I want to see grow. It also chugs along nicely on its own right now.

When there is a debate between whether we want to do something that’s going to make us more money or whether we want to do something that we think is going to move along the debate in politics, we choose the latter. At least I choose the latter. A lot of the guys want to as well.

We want to be influential in the political debate. It’s partly because of what you just said about the media environment, where there are so many different sources of information now that I think from a political perspective, it’s really difficult to get a message out to the electorate that everyone hears the same.

We’re not in the world where everyone’s going to watch the nightly news. When I was on the Obama campaign in ‘08, we knew that whatever events he did, we would judge the success of them through the prism of the three nightly news networks. That worked out pretty well for us as a campaign, even though we were on Facebook and trying to organize people on Facebook and do all that stuff back then.

It has been revealed that the way you judged the success of an event in a day was, “How did it play on the evening news?” That world is long gone. From the perspective of how we keep democracy together so that everyone is getting good, reliable information and that everyone is debating the same information, that’s just a really, really hard task. I see our job as trying to make that a little easier for people, at least on our side, on the left side of the political spectrum.

We want to be a place where people on the far left, people on the center left, Never Trumpers and people on the right can at least feel comfortable coming on, debating, talking to us because we’re trying to reconnect the civic discussion that has been just completely balkanized over the last 10 years.

My favorite example of what you’re describing is Zohran Mamdani. I don’t think he’s ever answered a question without saying he loves Fresh York City in the same way that Dr. Pimple Popper is always like, “I’m a dermatologist.” Literally just saying the first fact, reading his LinkedIn, because he can’t assume that you have any idea what’s going on. So “I love New York City” is just the first fact and then whatever answer. It comes up every single time.

That is partially an algorithmic problem. It’s partially just a media fragmentation problem. But you’re describing something bigger than that. You’re describing a shared value system. We might have different political ideas or different policy prescriptions, but we will agree that the Strait of Hormuz is closed.

In a recent development, we’re going to start there. That requires you to fight the algorithm. It requires you to fight the filter bubble. How do you take that approach? Are you just saying you love Newly introduced York City over and over again or is there something else?

You try to appear in a bunch of different information streams. You try to be on a whole bunch of different platforms. You try to go on a bunch of different shows. You try to have people on with all kinds of different perspectives from different parts of the political spectrum, just so that you’re cross-pollinating more with different audiences. That’s really crucial. We think about that as one strategy.

According to recent reports, but beyond that, it’s really difficult. People bemoan the demise of monoculture, and I think it’s not just a problem for entertainment and culture, or whatever it may be. It’s the biggest problem for politics. If there are no events, reveals, or moments in time where everyone in the country is focused on the same thing, consuming the same information, and consuming the same entertainment, that’s a problem for a society that needs to govern itself. I don’t think there’s a good solution for that, but that is something that at least we think about while we’re making decisions.

Industry observers note that the other viewpoint on this is actually Bari Weiss. I saw her do an interview with Jessica Lessin of The information a couple weeks ago and Bari’s argument is the media lost trust. It lost everyone’s trust by miscovering all this stuff and she thinks she needs to tear this down and rebuild it for the lost middle.

You can look at CBS’s ratings and decide whether or not that has been effective, but I hear that argument all the time — that this is actually a trust problem, that the media is lying to you. You can go online and you’ll hear the real truth about whatever it is. What do you make of that argument? What do you make of Bari Weiss making that argument?

According to recent reports, she’s right in that all of this is fundamentally a trust problem, but it’s not just a loss of trust in liberal media or what she would call liberal media. It’s a loss of trust in institutions across the board and across the political spectrum. It is fundamental to the rise of Donald Trump in the first place. We are now a low-trust society, even compared to other wealthy societies around the world.

You go to Scandinavia and these are much higher-trust societies. They handled Covid better. They handled the pandemic better because of that. America’s a very low-trust society. The balkanization of the media is a huge part of that. Even if you believe in one media institution, there’s another media institution that’s a competitor trying to tear that one down that’s going to tell you that they’re lying to you.

According to recent reports, the number of people I’ve talked to, and I also see this in focus groups all the time, where people will say, “I listen to Fox News and I watch Fox News and I also watch MS Now because I have to get both sides now.” People are now trying to seek out more partisan viewpoints or political viewpoints in order to make the judgments for themselves, which is a tough place to put individuals in. But because there’s so little trust in media in general, but also in the government and corporations, that’s what people are left to do.

There was a report last year in Semafor that you had held talks with The Bulwark to discuss a partnership. Obviously The Bulwark started as a bunch of Never Trumpers. Is that enough expansion? You’re going to have a shared set of facts and probably some different policy prescriptions?

In a recent development, the thing with The Bulwark is because they’re just so like-minded to us, we like doing a lot of stuff with them. Whether it makes sense as a business partnership you can put aside, because of the amount of cross-pollination between our shows. I’m always on Tim Miller’s podcast and he’s doing something with Lovett and Sarah Longwell’s doing something with Dan Pfeiffer.

Sources indicate that we think that by doing more stuff with them, their audience is exposed to us, our audience is exposed to them, and that just helps with our larger political mission. We see it more as a political alliance and partnership than it is a business partnership.

In a recent development, the reason I’m asking this is I see the creator businesses getting bigger. You can see the creators raising money to do roll-ups. I think Johnny Harris is raising money to roll up more YouTube channels. Right next to that is the platforms that hate this idea. The platforms would prefer the army of teenagers working for free.

In a recent development, the army of teenagers working for free never show up at YouTube’s door and say, “We would like better terms. We would like higher ad rates or we will withdraw our content.” It’s just, “We’re going to make more teenagers. You can leave.” We’ve seen this happen many times. Right now, something in the media ecosystem like Netflix is paying for podcasts and YouTube wants those people to stay.

Recent findings suggest that there’s something where the creator media has gravity. It has real audience, that audience is durable, and going from YouTube to Netflix might actually harm YouTube in some way. Whatever is happening there seems key. How do you think about Crooked in that dynamic? Would you ever go to YouTube and say, “We’re going to leave you for Netflix?”.

I have to say, once a bunch of podcasts were on Netflix and I started taking a spin through Netflix, I thought, “Even with the algorithm there, it’s really tricky to find those podcasts on Netflix.” Now, if you just have a really popular podcast and you have an audience, then that’s great.

But I just think that, at least from my perspective, it’s just easier to find your content on YouTube than it is on Netflix. I don’t think the money would be more valuable than the audience growth that you’d get on YouTube.

Industry observers note that to bring this all back around, I’ve heard you say these midterms represent the end of the Trump era. Whatever this was, it was blissfully over. All the politicians are now influencers unto themselves. JD Vance is a creature of X, for better or worse. That is how that man communicates. Mamdani is a creature of TikTok. Recent findings suggest that something has happened to our politics where this is how we communicate now. As you stated, the Democrats are a major tent. They have a lot of differing priorities. Do you think they will be able to effectively communicate in the platform environment, in the media environment that we find ourselves in now?

According to recent reports, that’s going to be difficult over the next two years. You still need a president, you need a leader of the party, to be able to try to effectively communicate. I got to know his speechwriter a little bit, and his campaign did something interesting there, which is they combined the speech writing and social media functions. They decided, “All right, this is a state rep in Texas who no one knows, and the way to become known is through storytelling. The oldest tactic in history.”.

Industry observers note that [Laughs] Are you really doing the end of Game of Thrones in my show right now, Jon? Come on. Don’t do this to me. No one liked it.

It has been revealed that if that story is compelling, then it will travel and break through even in this crowded media environment. Sources indicate that that is an effective way of getting people’s attention, but not necessarily holding their attention. If you are a politician today, you’ve got to figure out a way to get people’s attention, but then to hold it. And to hold it, you have to have a compelling story to tell.

I remember Democrats had a huge win in 2006, and then people can barely remember until the financial crisis what George Bush and the Democratic Congress were up to between 2006 and 2008, because everyone was focused on the Republican primary for president and the Democratic primary for president, because they were two wide open primaries. Because of the sexy spies. It’s right there.

San Francisco is just Milwaukee with rich people. I need to make this as clear as I can. It is not as scary as people want it to be.

There’s some very basic political science in here. Why we have a government is to counterbalance industry. Again, are we telling stories on social media? Abdul El-Sayed is doing political science 101 — “I’m a capitalist.”.

AI is the ultimate collective action problem or prisoner’s dilemma, whatever you want to call it. It’s people trying to figure out how to live together and divvy up scarce resources and figure out how to govern themselves.

That’s really messy and you actually need some social and political expertise to do that. You can’t just be a genius coder or a capitalist and feel like this is going to solve everything.
